text: By the time the moon had cleared the manor's east wing, they were already inside it, which was rather the point — Marian had made it plain, several times and with increasing firmness, that discussing a plan at length was a fine way to talk yourselves out of the nerve required to execute one.

Will went first, because Will going first was, by now, simply how things were done — straight through the front gate in a stolen steward's coat, informing the one drowsy guard on duty that he was expected, with such total conviction that the guard let him through if only to avoid the discomfort of arguing about it. The rest came in after, through a side door Marian had located earlier that afternoon with the unhurried thoroughness of a woman casing a building the way other people admired scenery.

“Strongbox will be the study,” Brother Crumb murmured, leading them with the confidence of a man who had, by his own admission, spent considerable time thinking about where wealthy men kept their excess. “Man like Vane wants his coin close enough to admire it. Vanity, mostly. Works in our favor.”
“You keep saying that like it's a professional opinion,” Long John whispered.
“It's an informed opinion,” said Crumb. “There's a difference, and the difference is mostly that nobody's paying me for this one.”

sequence._describe: Comedic chaos inside the manor at night: Robin of Loxby's arrow knocking down a tapestry onto a guard, Long John Little squeezing through a too-small doorway, Will Scarlett-Sleeves distracting a second guard with animated conversation, all happening simultaneously in different parts of a dim corridor. Warm painterly storybook illustration style, expressive and slightly exaggerated proportions, rich saturated color, soft painterly brushwork, comedic tone. Wide shot capturing multiple comedic vignettes, 3:2 landscape aspect ratio, dim nighttime interior lighting, lively caper energy.

text: What followed had the shape of every job they'd ever half-planned and mostly improvised, which was to say: chaotic, faintly miraculous, and somehow effective despite itself. Robin, tasked with watching the corridor, loosed a warning shot at a shape in the dark that turned out to be a coat rack, and in doing so knocked a hanging tapestry down directly over the one guard who'd actually heard something and come to investigate — who spent the next several minutes fighting his way out from under a great deal of heavy embroidered fabric while the source of his suspicion strolled past unbothered.

Long John, wedged for one genuinely alarming moment in a doorway not built for a man his size, extracted himself with a soft pop and an apology to the doorframe that nobody had time to appreciate properly. Will kept up a running conversation with a second guard about wine cellars, entirely invented, entirely convincing, walking the man in the opposite direction from everyone else with the easy patience of a born liar.
Marian reached the study first, and had the strongbox's lock defeated within a span of time that made Robin, arriving a moment later, feel faintly embarrassed on behalf of locks in general.
“That's not an honest skill,” he said.

“Neither is tax farming,” said Marian, without looking up, “and yet here we are, correcting the balance.” The lock gave with a small, satisfying click. Inside sat considerably more coin than even Crumb's optimistic estimate had suggested — neat stacks of it, orderly in the particular way of a man who enjoyed counting his own wealth more than was strictly healthy.
“There's more here than we need,” Robin said, already dividing it by eye.

“Take what we need,” said Marian, “and precisely that. We're not thieves for the sport of it.” She began counting out the exact sum, coin by coin, with the fastidious care of a woman who intended the math to be unimpeachable even if nothing else about the evening was.

sequence._describe: Vane standing furious in the doorway of his study, fully dressed with a lit candle in hand, having just discovered the crew mid-heist, a shattered vase visible on the floor nearby, tone shifting sharply from comic to serious. text: It was, in the end, Barley's cousin in spirit — an entirely unrelated and entirely unlucky manor cat — that gave them away, streaking across the hall in pursuit of something only it could see and colliding directly with a side table bearing, among other things, a very large and very unstable vase.
The sound it made going down was not subtle.

Vane was awake, dressed, and in the doorway of his own study within a span of time that suggested he slept a great deal lighter than his comfortable circumstances would suggest, a lit candle in one hand and an expression that moved, in rapid succession, from confusion to comprehension to a fury that had nowhere near enough patience left in it for negotiation.
“Guards!” he bellowed, and the manor, which had until that moment been a place of quiet and easily-managed chaos, became something considerably less forgiving.
“That's our cue,” said Will, with the particular calm of a man who had decided, wisely, that panicking would take time they didn't have.

They ran. It was not, this time, the loose and mostly-comic running that had carried them through tax squares and forest search parties — this was something with real teeth in it, boots pounding on stone behind them, a household roused and furious and considerably better armed than a highwayman's opportunistic band. Marian led with the coin secured against her, counting exits in her head faster than she could voice them. Robin's bow found his hand without conscious thought, though there was, this time, no room in him for the easy confidence that had carried him through smaller dangers.
Vane's voice followed them down the hall, no longer merely angry but promising — cold, precise, the voice of a man who intended to remember every one of their faces at his leisure.

text: The side door Marian had scouted that afternoon was, by the time they reached it, no longer the quiet exit it had been — two guards stood between them and the night air, drawn swords catching what little moonlight made it through the manor's high windows.

Long John didn't slow down. He simply arrived, all momentum and desperate necessity, and the two guards discovered, in the half-second available to them, that a very large man moving at speed does not require finesse to be effective. They went down together, tangled, cursing, and very much alive but entirely out of the way, which was all anyone had asked of the moment.
“Go!” Long John roared, already turning to hold the doorway a second longer than his own escape strictly allowed.

“Not without you,” said Robin, and for once — for the first time all evening — nobody argued with the sentiment, they simply made it true, dragging him bodily through the gap before the guards could untangle themselves and give chase.

They didn't stop running until the manor's lights had shrunk to something small and impotent behind them, and even then it was less a decision to stop than a collective realization that their bodies had simply run out of road to give.

Brother Crumb, doubled over and wheezing in a manner that suggested his talents lay considerably more in cooking than in cardiovascular endurance, managed, between breaths: “I would like it — noted — for the record — that I said the study, and I was right about the study.”
“Nobody's disputing the study,” Marian said, still clutching the coin, checking it by feel in the dark as though it might have escaped somewhere during the chase. “We're disputing the vase.”
“The vase,” said Will, with real feeling, “was not part of the plan.”
“Neither was any of the rest of it,” said Marian. “And yet.”

text: They counted the coin twice more once they'd put real distance behind them, in the grey hour before proper dawn, and found it — against every reasonable expectation for a night that had gone that badly wrong — exactly right. Precisely enough to clear the Weavers' debt, not a coin more taken than the sum required.

It should have felt like a victory. It mostly did, in the tired, aching, thoroughly relieved way that victories generally feel once the running stops. But Robin found himself thinking, more than once on the long walk back, of the particular quality in Vane's voice as they'd fled — not merely angry, but patient, in the specific way of a man confident the account wasn't closed simply because the coin was gone.
“He got a good look at us,” Robin said, finally, to no one in particular.
“He did,” Marian agreed, not slowing her pace. “That's a problem for after we've saved a family's roof. Not before.”
“And after?”
Marian didn't answer that one directly, which, by now, everyone present understood well enough to recognize as an answer of its own.
